I'm 52, been farming these lands in Quzhou County since I was a teenager. My father taught me, and I've seen what works on the North China Plain. We have good irrigation here, and the soil is decent loam, so the double-cropping system of winter wheat followed by summer maize is still the most reliable way to put food on the table and earn some cash. I don't see any reason to change what's worked for decades.

I have 8 mu of land. I'll plant all of it with winter wheat this autumn — it's already almost time. I'll use an improved wheat variety that the local seed station recommends; it resists lodging and has decent yield. For the summer, I'll follow with hybrid maize right after the wheat harvest — no rest for the land, that's how we do it here. I'll use rotary tillage before wheat sowing to break up the stubble from last year's maize and prepare a fine seedbed. For the maize, I'll do minimal tillage after wheat harvest to save time and moisture.

For fertilizer, I'll apply compound fertilizer at sowing and top-dress with urea at jointing for the wheat. The maize will get base fertilizer and a side-dressing at the big flare stage. Irrigation is critical: the wheat will need water at sowing, then again at jointing, and once at grain filling — three times total. The maize will need one good irrigation at the big flare stage, maybe another if July gets too dry, but usually the summer rains help. I'll spray pesticides two or three times for each crop to control aphids, powdery mildew on wheat, and corn borer on maize. I expect about 500 kg per mu of wheat and 600 kg per mu of maize if the weather cooperates.
